title: Earthquake-Resistant Design
keyIdea: We cannot stop earthquakes, but we can design for them. Diagonal cross-bracing turns square frames into triangles, which keep their shape when pushed. A weak open ground floor (a soft storey) must be braced, because it holds up every floor above. Base isolation puts rubber bearings between a building and the ground, so less shaking reaches the rooms. Near the coast, seismometers and ocean buoys feed a tsunami warning centre, which sends sirens and phone alerts. Evacuation plans and drills mean people know to go to high ground fast.
familyTip: Build a cube frame from straws and pipe cleaners or lolly sticks and sticky tack. Push the top: it folds over. Tape one diagonal on each side and push again. Then look up your local emergency plan together, or if you live near a coast, find the tsunami evacuation route and the nearest high ground on a map.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: brace a frame and a tower, run shake tests, fit rubber bearings, order the tsunami warning chain and pick a safe escape route.

kid: In an earthquake the ground moves back and forth. A building moves with it. A frame shaped like a square can lean over, because its corners turn like hinges. Add one diagonal beam and the square becomes two triangles. A triangle cannot change shape, so the frame stays upright. Builders call these beams cross-braces.

The ground floor holds up all the floors above it, so it gets the biggest push. A ground floor with big shop windows and no walls is the weak spot. Many buildings have fallen down because that floor folded. Brace it first, then brace the rest.

Some buildings sit on thick rubber pads called bearings. When the ground shakes, it slides about under the pads. The building on top moves slowly and gently, so things inside stay put. Hospitals and museums often use them.

An earthquake under the sea can push up a giant wave called a tsunami. Machines called seismometers feel the quake, and buoys out at sea sense the wave. A warning centre checks the readings and sends sirens and phone alerts. If you are at the coast and feel a long, strong quake, do not wait for the siren. Go to high ground on foot straight away. Schools practise drills, so everyone knows the way.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. This matches NGSS 4-ESS3-2: generate and compare solutions that reduce the impact of natural Earth processes on people. The standard's own examples are earthquake-resistant buildings and better warning systems. It also uses the 3-5-ETS1 engineering practices and supports the earthquakes and tsunamis work in Key Stage 2 geography in England. Key words: earthquake, seismometer, cross-bracing, soft storey, base isolation, rubber bearing, tsunami, warning centre, buoy, evacuation, drill, high ground.

The lab has five tasks. Children push a pin-jointed square frame until it leans, then add a diagonal and find it will not move. They brace a five-floor tower with an open shop floor and run a shake test that cracks every unbraced floor. They fit rubber bearings under a building and see a vase stay on a table that tipped over before. Then they put the tsunami warning chain in order and choose the escape road that climbs to a hilltop instead of following the coast or a river.

Common mistakes. Children often think a heavier or stronger building is always safer. In fact, mass high up increases the forces in a quake; the real fixes are bracing, isolation and dampers. Other slips: bracing the top floor instead of the open ground floor, thinking a building should be bolted rigidly to the ground, waiting for a siren after a long, strong quake at the coast, and going to look at the sea. Be careful with Drop, Cover and Hold On: it is for while the ground shakes. The tsunami evacuation starts once the shaking stops.

practice.prompt: Why does a square frame with one diagonal brace stay upright when pushed?
choices: The brace makes two triangles, and a triangle cannot change shape
The brace makes the frame heavier
The brace glues the corners so they never turn
practice.hint: In the lab, what shapes did the frame turn into once the diagonal was in?
practice.explain: The diagonal splits the square into two triangles. A triangle's three sides fix its angles, so the frame cannot lean.

practice.prompt: Each floor of a tower needs one X-brace, made of 2 diagonal beams. How many diagonal beams are needed for {n} floors?
practice.hint: Every floor uses 2 beams. Multiply the number of floors by 2.

practice.prompt: A tsunami will reach the town in {t} minutes. Walking to the hilltop takes {w} minutes. How many minutes are left to spare?
practice.hint: Take the walking time away from the time before the wave arrives.
practice.explain: {t} − {w} = {=t-w} minutes to spare. Going at once keeps that spare time.

practice.prompt: A building has an open ground floor of shops with no walls. Which floor should be braced first?
practice.hint: Which floor holds up every floor above it?
practice.explain: The ground floor carries the push from every floor above, so an open one is the weak spot that fails first.

practice.prompt: What do rubber bearings between a building and the ground do in an earthquake?
choices: Let the ground move under the building, so less shaking reaches it
Fix the building more tightly to the ground
practice.hint: In the lab, what happened to the vase once the bearings were in?
practice.explain: The bearings let the ground slide about underneath, so the rooms above move slowly and gently. This is called base isolation.

pool.prompt: Which shape do builders use to stop frames leaning?
pool.hint: Which shape could not lean when you pushed it in the lab?
pool.explain: A triangle cannot change shape without bending a side, so braces turn squares into triangles.

pool.prompt: What does a seismometer do in a tsunami warning system?
choices: It feels the earthquake and records how strong it is
It sounds the siren in the town
pool.hint: Which link in the warning chain senses the earthquake?
pool.explain: Seismometers feel the ground shaking and send readings to the warning centre, which decides whether to warn people.

pool.prompt: Put these in order: A alerts go out, B sensors pick up the quake, C warning centre checks the data. Which order is right?
pool.hint: Something must be measured before it can be checked, and checked before people are told.
pool.explain: Sensors pick it up, the warning centre checks the data, and then the alerts go out.

pool.prompt: You are at the beach and feel a long, strong earthquake. There is no siren. What should you do?
choices: Go to high ground on foot straight away
Wait until you hear the siren
Go down to look at the sea
pool.hint: A long, strong quake at the coast is itself a warning.
pool.explain: The wave can arrive before any siren. Go as high or as far inland as you can, straight away.

pool.prompt: Why is a bridge over a river near the coast a bad place to go in a tsunami?
choices: Tsunami waves rush up rivers, and the bridge is low
pool.hint: In the lab, why was River Lane the wrong road?
pool.explain: A tsunami travels up rivers and floods low ground nearby, so a low bridge over the water is exposed.

pool.prompt: Ella says a building fixed rigidly to the ground is always the safest. What is the problem?
choices: It shakes as hard as the ground; bearings can let the ground move underneath
pool.hint: What happened to the vase when the building had no bearings?
pool.explain: A building fixed to the ground passes the shaking straight up. Base isolation lets the ground move under it, so the rooms shake less.

pool.prompt: Why do schools practise earthquake and tsunami drills?
choices: So everyone knows what to do and where to go without stopping to think
pool.hint: In a real emergency there is little time to plan.
pool.explain: Drills make the plan a habit, so people act fast and safely when a real quake or warning comes.

pool.prompt: A building stands on {r} rows of columns with {k} columns in each row. Each column needs one rubber bearing. How many bearings are needed?
pool.hint: Multiply the number of rows by the number of columns in each row.
pool.explain: {r} rows × {k} columns = {=r*k} bearings, one under every column.

pool.prompt: In the deep ocean a tsunami can travel about 700 km in an hour. How far can it travel in {h} hours, in km?
pool.hint: Each hour adds another 700 km. Multiply 700 by {h}.
pool.explain: 700 × {h} = {=700*h} km. That is why warnings are sent to coasts far from the earthquake.
